content: During the 1950s and 1960s, the Soviet Union conducted numerous space missions involving dogs to assess the feasibility of human spaceflight. At least 57 dogs were used in these experiments, though the actual number of individual dogs was smaller, as some participated in multiple flights. Most of the dogs survived, with fatalities primarily resulting from technical malfunctions. Training of the Dogs Dogs were chosen for these experiments because scientists believed they could better endure prolonged periods of inactivity. Stray dogs were specifically selected over domesticated ones, as they were thought to be more resilient to the harsh conditions of space travel. Female dogs were preferred due to their temperament and because the suits designed to collect waste were tailored for females. The training regimen for these dogs was rigorous. They were confined in small boxes for 15 to 20 days at a time, trained to remain still for extended periods, and accustomed to wearing space suits. They were also placed in simulators mimicking rocket launches, subjected to centrifuges to simulate the high accelerations of launch, and kept in progressively smaller cages to prepare them for the cramped conditions of space capsules. Dogs that flew in orbit were fed a jelly-like protein-rich food designed to aid digestion during long periods of inactivity. Sub-Orbital Flights Dezik and Tsygan Dezik and Tsygan were the first dogs to undertake a sub-orbital flight on July 22, 1951, reaching an altitude of 100 km. Both dogs survived the mission. Tsygan was later adopted by Soviet physicist Anatoli Blagonravov. Dezik flew again in September 1951 with another dog, Lisa, but neither survived this subsequent mission. Lisa and Ryzhik Lisa and Ryzhik flew to an altitude of 100 km on June 2, 1954. Both dogs successfully completed the mission. Smelaya and Malyshka Smelaya, whose name means Bold, was scheduled for a flight in September 1951 but went missing the day before launch. She was found the next day and successfully flew with another dog, Malyshka (Little One). Bolik and ZIB Bolik escaped just days before her scheduled flight in September 1951. A stray dog, later named ZIB (an acronym for Substitute for Missing Bolik), was hastily recruited and successfully completed the mission despite having no prior training. Otvazhnaya and Snezhinka Otvazhnaya (Brave One) flew on July 2, 1959, alongside a rabbit named Marfusha (Martha) and another dog, Snezhinka (Snowflake). Otvazhnaya went on to participate in five additional flights between 1959 and 1960. Albina and Tsyganka Albina and Tsyganka (Gypsy Girl) were ejected from their capsule at an altitude of 85 km and landed safely. Albina was considered for the Sputnik 2 mission but was ultimately not selected for orbital flight. Damka and Krasavka Damka (Little Lady) and Krasavka (Little Beauty) were scheduled for an orbital flight on December 22, 1960. However, the upper stage rocket failed, resulting in an unplanned sub-orbital flight. Both dogs were recovered unharmed. Damka was also known by the names Shutka (Joke) and Zhemchuzhnaya (Pearly), while Krasavka was also called Kometka (Little Comet) and Zhulka (Cheater). Other dogs that participated in sub-orbital flights included Dymka (Smoky), Modnitsa (Fashionable), and Kozyavka (Little Gnat). At least four other dogs flew in September 1951, though two or more were lost during these missions. Orbital Flights Laika Laika, originally named Kudryavka (Little Curly), became the first living Earth-born creature to orbit the planet aboard Sputnik 2 on November 3, 1957. She was also known by the names Zhuchka (Little Beetle) and Limonchik (Lemon). The American media nicknamed her Muttnik. Laika died between five and seven hours into the flight due to stress and overheating. The true cause of her death was not disclosed until 2002; earlier reports falsely claimed she had been euthanized or died from oxygen depletion. The scientist responsible for the mission later expressed regret for her death. Bars and Lisichka Bars (Panther or Lynx) and Lisichka (Little Fox) perished when their rocket exploded 28.5 seconds after launch on July 28, 1960. Belka and Strelka Belka (Squirrel or Whitey) and Strelka (Little Arrow) spent a day in orbit aboard Korabl-Sputnik-2 (Sputnik 5) on August 19, 1960, and safely returned to Earth. They were accompanied by a rabbit, 42 mice, 2 rats, flies, and various plants and fungi. All passengers survived. Strelka later gave birth to six puppies, one of which, Pushinka (Fluffy), was gifted to U.S. President John F. Kennedy's daughter by Nikita Khrushchev. Pushinka and a Kennedy family dog named Charlie had four puppies, humorously referred to as pupniks by JFK. Pchelka and Mushka Pchelka (Little Bee) and Mushka (Little Fly) orbited Earth on December 1, 1960, aboard Korabl-Sputnik-3 (Sputnik 6). Their spacecraft disintegrated during re-entry on December 2, killing all aboard. Mushka had previously been trained for Sputnik 2 but was excluded from the mission due to her refusal to eat. Chernushka Chernushka (Blackie) completed one orbit aboard Korabl-Sputnik-4 (Sputnik 9) on March 9, 1961. She was accompanied by a cosmonaut dummy named Ivan Ivanovich, mice, and a guinea pig. The dummy was ejected during re-entry and landed safely via parachute, while Chernushka was recovered unharmed inside the capsule. Zvezdochka Zvezdochka (Little Star), named by Yuri Gagarin, completed one orbit aboard Sputnik 10 on March 25, 1961. This was the final test flight before Gagarin's historic mission. Zvezdochka and the cosmonaut dummy aboard were both recovered safely. Veterok and Ugolyok Veterok (Little Breeze) and Ugolyok (Little Piece of Coal) were launched on February 22, 1966, aboard Cosmos 110. They spent 22 days in orbit, setting a record for the longest spaceflight by dogs. This record was not surpassed by humans until the Skylab 2 mission in June 1973.
